The '''1660 Ayuman Cup''', recognised retrospectively as the 2nd edition of the '''[[FLLA World Cup]]''', was an international [[Arraby]] tournament contested by the senior men's national teams of the leading Ayuman football associations. It was held in [[Easuhura]], across [[Ayuma]], from 5 June to 4 July 1660, and was won by [[Lycroa]], who defeated [[Emara]] 6–1 in the [[#Final|final]] at the Bokayek Grand Stadium to claim their first title. The scoreline remains the most emphatic in a final in the competition's history.<ref name="heritage-overview">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1660/overview|title=The 1660 Ayuman Cup: tournament overview|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 June 1763}}</ref>

The competition was staged under the older title of the Ayuman Cup, the name it bore before the [[FLLA]] was constituted and the contest was relaunched and renamed the [[FLLA World Cup]] at the [[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700 edition]]. The seven continental confederations that later structured the competition did not yet exist, and all eight entrants were drawn from [[Ayuma]]; the finals were organised not by any standing body but by a congress of the Ayuman national associations, the informal arrangement under which the early editions were run.<ref name="heritage-rename">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/history/early-competition-names|title=From the Ayuman Cup to the FLLA World Cup: the early names of the competition|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=12 February 1764}}</ref>

The 1660 edition was contested for the '''[[FLLA World Cup#The Ayuma Cup|Ayuma Cup]]''', the original rotating trophy of the competition, which had been introduced at the inaugural [[1656 FLLA World Cup|1656 edition]] and was presented to the victorious side at the close of each tournament. It was the second and last edition at which the Ayuma Cup was contested: the trophy was retired in 1668 on the introduction of the original [[FLLA World Cup#The Andah Cup|Andah Cup]], and was carried back to [[Lycroa]] by the champions, who as its last holders retained it. The Ayuma Cup survives in a museum collection; it was the original Andah Cup, used from 1668, that was destroyed in [[Alzurian Union|Alzuria]] in 1688. No bespoke permanent trophy yet existed, the permanent-trophy tradition beginning only at the [[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700 edition]].<ref name="heritage-trophy">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/trophies/the-ayuma-cup|title=The Ayuma Cup and its early history|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=2 July 1764}}</ref>

==Host selection==

The 1660 tournament was awarded to [[Easuhura]] by a congress of the Ayuman national associations, the informal body that organised the competition before the foundation of the [[FLLA]]. With only the inaugural [[1656 FLLA World Cup|1656 edition]] behind it, the competition had no established hosting rotation, and the award to Easuhura reflected the readiness of its associations to provide grounds for a larger field than the first tournament had assembled. The Easuhuran organisers undertook to stage the finals across five cities, with the principal matches held in [[Bokayek]].<ref name="heritage-host">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1660/host|title=1660 Ayuman Cup: the award of hosting rights to Easuhura|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 June 1763}}</ref>

==Format==

The 8 entered teams were divided into two groups of four for the group stage. Each group operated on a single round-robin basis, with each team playing the other three sides in its group; two points were awarded for a win and one for a draw, in line with the scoring system then in use. The top two teams in each group advanced to the [[#Knockout stage|knockout stage]], while the bottom two were eliminated. Where teams finished level on points, places were determined first by goal difference and then by goals scored.

The knockout stage consisted of two semi-finals and the [[#Final|final]], each played as a single-elimination tie over 90 minutes. A tie level at the end of normal time was extended by a single 30-minute period of [[wikipedia:Extra time|extra time]]; under the regulations of the period, any tie still level after extra time was to be settled by a replay rather than by a [[wikipedia:Penalty shoot-out (association football)|penalty shoot-out]], a procedure not yet in use. No replay proved necessary in 1660.

==Participating teams==

Eight teams took part in the 1660 finals, all of them Ayuman national associations. The continental confederations that later structured the [[FLLA World Cup]] had not yet been established, and qualification was settled under the informal arrangements of the period; as host nation, [[Easuhura]] took part automatically. The participating teams were:<ref name="heritage-teams">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1660/teams|title=1660 Ayuman Cup: participating teams|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=18 June 1763}}</ref>

==Venues==

Five stadiums in five host cities, all in [[Easuhura]], were used in the final tournament. The principal venue was the Bokayek Grand Stadium in [[Bokayek]], which staged the opening match and the final and was the largest ground in use. The two semi-finals were divided between the Sokhan Arena in [[Sokhan]] and the Lachon Stadium in [[Lachon]]. The remaining group-stage fixtures were shared between these grounds, Paviri Park in [[Paviri]] and the smallest venue, the Chayek Field in [[Chayek]].<ref name="heritage-venues">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1660/venues|title=Host stadiums of the 1660 Ayuman Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=18 June 1763}}</ref>

==Squads==

Each participating association registered a squad of eighteen players, two of whom were required to be goalkeepers; the smaller squads of the period reflected the limited substitution rules then in force, under which a single replacement was permitted only for an injured goalkeeper. A total of 144 players were registered for the tournament.<ref name="heritage-squads">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1660/squads|title=1660 Ayuman Cup: registered squads|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=18 June 1763}}</ref>

==Match officials==

The organising congress appointed a panel of referees and linesmen drawn from the associations not represented in the latter stages of the competition. The opening match was refereed by Tomas Veld of [[Verusa]], and the final by Mikol Drenn of [[Eldjo]], the senior official of the tournament. The small officiating pool of the period meant that several referees took charge of fixtures involving teams from neighbouring associations, though never from their own.<ref name="heritage-officials">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1660/officials|title=Match officials of the 1660 Ayuman Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=18 June 1763}}</ref>

==Group stage==

The two groups were each contested as a single round-robin. The top two teams in each group advanced to the knockout stage; points were awarded on the two-points-for-a-win system in use at the time, with goal difference and then goals scored used to separate teams level on points.

All dates are given in the local time of the host cities.

==Knockout stage==

The knockout stage involved the four teams that advanced from the group stage, with each group winner drawn against the runner-up of the other group. Ties level after 90 minutes were extended by a single period of [[wikipedia:Extra time|extra time]]; both semi-finals were settled inside normal time, and no tie required a replay.

===Final===

The final was held at the Bokayek Grand Stadium on 4 July 1660 before an estimated crowd of 15,000. [[Lycroa]] took an early lead through Edmar Calvik, the tournament's leading scorer, and were 3–0 ahead before [[Emara]] replied through Edmund Crale; Calvik went on to complete a hat-trick, with two goals from Joren Edrin and a late one from Mern Holt, for a 6–1 finish. The margin remains the largest recorded in a final of the competition, and the victory secured Lycroa's first title; the [[FLLA World Cup#The Ayuma Cup|Ayuma Cup]] was presented to the Lycroan captain at the close of the match.<ref name="heritage-final">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1660/final|title=The 1660 Ayuman Cup final: Lycroa 6–1 Emara|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 June 1763}}</ref>

==Statistics==

===Goalscorers===

A total of 85 goals were scored in 16 matches, an average of 5.31 per match. The leading scorer was the Lycroan forward Edmar Calvik, who scored fourteen goals across the tournament, including a hat-trick in the final. No formal individual awards were presented at the 1660 edition: the leading-player, top-scorer and best-goalkeeper prizes (the [[FLLA World Cup#Awards|Vairan Ball, Marskval and Bastion]]) were not instituted until the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 edition]], and the figures below are recognised retrospectively in the [[FLLA]]'s heritage records.<ref name="heritage-stats">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/world-cup/1660/statistics|title=1660 Ayuman Cup statistical record|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=18 June 1763}}</ref>

==Trophy and significance==

The 1660 edition was only the second tournament in the competition's history, following the inaugural [[1656 FLLA World Cup|1656 edition]], and the first to be staged with a field of eight teams. Lycroa's 6–1 victory over Emara is remembered as the most one-sided final the competition has produced, and the result established Lycroa as one of the strongest of the early Ayuman sides. That the hosts, Easuhura, reached the semi-finals and took third place rather than the title was in keeping with a competition in which the host nation has rarely prevailed.<ref name="heritage-overview" />

The cup that Lycroa lifted was the [[FLLA World Cup#The Ayuma Cup|Ayuma Cup]], the original rotating trophy, which had been introduced at the inaugural edition four years earlier. The 1660 edition was the second and last at which it was contested: it was retired in 1668 on the introduction of the original [[FLLA World Cup#The Andah Cup|Andah Cup]], and as its last holders Lycroa retained it. It was the Andah Cup, used from 1668, that was finally lost when it was destroyed in [[Alzurian Union|Alzuria]] in 1688; when the competition was relaunched and renamed the [[FLLA World Cup]] at the [[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700 edition]], no rotating cup was available, and the permanent-trophy tradition that has characterised the competition ever since was begun in its place.<ref name="heritage-trophy" />

The edition that had been scheduled to follow in 1664, awarded to [[Alzurian Union|Alzuria]], was later cancelled because of the [[Great Imperial War]], and the competition did not resume until the [[1668 FLLA World Cup|1668 edition]]. The 1660 tournament was thus the last edition contested for eight years.<ref name="heritage-rename" />
